title: Have you ever, and have you already
goal: Use *har* + the supine for experiences and results — and know when Swedish chooses it instead of the simple past.
bekal: the supine: a form that only lives alongside *har* and *hade*
when to use *har gjort* and when to use *gjorde*
talking about experiences: ever, never, just

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Har du sett norrsken?
dialogs.intro: A November evening. Dian, Elin and Oskar are sitting in the dorm kitchen. Outside, it is already minus six.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Har du varit i Norrland någon gång?
lines.id: Have you ever been to Norrland?
lines.literal: have you been in Norrland some time?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nej, jag har aldrig varit norr om Uppsala.
lines.id: No, I've never been north of Uppsala.
lines.literal: no, I have never been north of Uppsala.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Då har du inte sett norrsken heller.
lines.id: Then you haven't seen the northern lights either.
lines.literal: then have you not seen north-light either.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Ja, många gånger. Vi åkte till Kiruna varje vinter när jag var liten.
lines.id: Yes, lots of times. We went to Kiruna every winter when I was little.
lines.literal: yes, many times. we went to Kiruna every winter when I was little.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Jag har bott där i två år. Jag jobbade på gruvan.
lines.id: I've lived there for two years. I worked at the mine.
lines.literal: I have lived there in two years. I worked at mine-the.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Har du gjort det? Det visste jag inte!
lines.literal: have you done that? that knew I not!

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Jag har aldrig berättat det. Det var före universitetet.
lines.id: I've never told anyone. It was before university.
lines.literal: I have never told it. it was before university-the.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.id: Have you two ever eaten surströmming, by the way?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nej, och jag har hört tillräckligt om den.
lines.id: No, and I've heard enough about it.
lines.literal: no, and I have heard enough about it.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Klokt. Jag har provat en gång. En gång räcker.
lines.id: Wise. I've tried it once. Once is enough.
lines.literal: wise. I have tried one time. one time suffices.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Vi har precis bestämt: nästa vinter åker vi norrut allihop.
lines.id: We've just decided: next winter we're all going up north.
lines.literal: we have just decided: next winter go we northward all-of-us.

notes: **The supine never stands alone.** It always comes after *har* (have) or *hade* (had). Its form never changes — not for the person, not for gender, not for number. *Jag har varit, du har varit, vi har varit*. Good news: no "has" versus "have" either — *har* is the same for everyone.

**Har varit vs var.** The difference is much the same as in English: *har varit* talks about an **experience with no specific time** ("have been"), while *var* talks about **an event at a specific time** ("was"). *Jag har varit i Kiruna* (I have been to Kiruna) vs *Jag var i Kiruna förra vintern* (I was in Kiruna last winter). As soon as there is a clear time expression, the simple past is used — exactly as in English.

**Aldrig + har = never.** *Jag har aldrig varit där* — notice that *aldrig* stands **after** *har* and **before** the supine, exactly where *inte* goes. This is the same pattern as the helper verbs in Unit 8 — and conveniently, it matches English "I have never been".

**Norrsken** — the aurora borealis, literally "north light". It can be seen in the northern third of Sweden on around two hundred nights a year, and it is the main reason people visit Kiruna and Abisko in winter.

**Surströmming** is herring fermented in a can until the can bulges. Its smell is one of the strongest in the food world, and Swedes open it outdoors, underwater, while laughing at the faces of newcomers. Turning it down is entirely acceptable; trying it once will win you acceptance anywhere in northern Sweden.

**Precis bestämt** — *precis* with the *har* form means "just": *jag har precis kommit* (I've just arrived). This is one place where the *har* form is used for something that clearly just happened, because the focus is on **the result now**, not the event itself — just like English "I've just arrived".

grammars.title: The supine by verb group
after: The pattern is beautifully tidy: **group 1 takes *-at*, group 2 takes *-t*, group 3 takes *-tt*, group 4 (strong) takes *-it*.** Four endings, four groups, no exceptions at A1 level.

Strong verbs use **the vowel of the basic form**, not the vowel of the past: *skriva → skrev → skrivit* (not *skrevit*), *dricka → drack → druckit*, *sitta → satt → suttit*. Notice the *u* that turns up in some supines — a leftover of the same ancient pattern that gives English *drink–drank–drunk* and *sing–sang–sung*.
Some of the most common forms: **varit** (vara), **haft** (ha), **gjort** (göra), **gått** (gå), **kommit** (komma), **sett** (se), **fått** (få), **tagit** (ta), **sagt** (säga), **blivit** (bli).

grammars.title: Har gjort or gjorde

head: Use *har* + supine when…
Example
Use the simple past when…
Example
rows: talking about an experience with no time given
telling events in sequence in the past
Jag **tappade** nyckeln och **letade** i en timme.

after: The practical rule: **if your sentence contains a time expression pointing to a specific moment in the past, use the simple past.** *Igår*, *förra veckan*, *i helgen*, *klockan tre* — they all call for *gjorde*, not *har gjort*. It is the same instinct that stops you saying "I have done it yesterday" in English.

The form **hade + supine** ("had done") exists too and works exactly like English *had done*: *När jag kom hade de redan ätit* (when I arrived they had already eaten). You won't use it much at A1, but you will recognize it from the pattern.

head: Svenska
English
rows: Har du varit i Sverige förut?
Have you been to Sweden before?
Hur länge har du bott här?
How long have you lived here?
Jag har bott här i sex månader.
I've lived here for six months.

blocks.text: The last two rows show a spot where Swedish and English **agree**: for something that started in the past and **is still going on**, Swedish uses *har bott* — just like English *have lived*, and unlike many other European languages, such as German and French, which use the present tense here. So if "How long have you lived here?" feels natural to you, the Swedish will too. The pattern is the same.

blocks.title: Än, redan, fortfarande
items: **än** — yet, used in negative sentences and questions: *Har du ätit än?* · *Jag har inte bestämt än.*
**inte längre** — no longer, not anymore: *Hon bor inte längre här.*
These four words cover almost every conversation about what has and hasn't happened yet.

sections.title: Northern Sweden, and a real winter

blocks.text: In Kiruna, Sweden's northernmost town, the sun **doesn't rise at all** for about twenty days in December, and **doesn't set at all** for about fifty days in summer. Locals call the dark period *polarnatt* and the bright one *midnattssol*. The town itself is being moved three kilometers east, building by building, because the iron-ore mine beneath it is making the ground sink.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 14
items: Say the whole checkout conversation from memory, from *hej* to *detsamma*.
Then turn it into a story in the past: *Jag handlade på ICA, jag köpte ost, jag betalade med kort.*
Finally, turn it again into the experience form: *Jag har handlat på ICA många gånger. Jag har aldrig betalat med kontanter.*
